description: We are a team based from Granite Bay High School. Individuals with extensive full‑stack app development or machine learning experience are welcome to join us and help us with our challenge.
summary: NISAR’s radar sees rice fields through the summer clouds that blind ordinary satellites, but teaching a computer to recognise rice takes labelled examples, which are scarce and years old. MaskSAR uses NISAR’s first public season to find a novel way around that shortage: we let models first learn the rhythm of the growing season from unlabelled NISAR data, then check whether that knowledge holds up with few labels, missing scans, and a new continent. In China’s Sanjiang Plain, we trained more than 2,000 models, from temporal transformers and a spatial vision transformer to a temporal CNN and gradient boosting, and scored each only on land it had never seen. Transformers that first learned from unlabelled radar beat the CNN and gradient boosting at matching the crop map of a region where only a few hundred labeled examples were available, and held up far better when satellite passes were missing. We then moved the models, unchanged, to California’s Sacramento Valley. When scan dates matched the season they had learned, they produced a usable first map without seeing a single California label, picking out 90% of the rice on the official 2025 US crop map. For agricultural analysts and researchers, this shows when pretraining pays off and how to start mapping a new region before local labels exist. MaskSAR Explorer, our interactive app, lets scientists and interested learners explore both regions’ radar and inspect their evidence at sample locations.
details:
MaskSAR is a research study and an interactive app that combines radar data, machine learning, and temporal visualisations to apply SAR data to agriculture science and space technology education. NISAR’s L-band radar sees rice fields through clouds, but the labels needed to train crop-mapping models are scarce and outdated in many countries. Using NISAR’s first season, we created a model that learns to map rice fields from only a few hundred labels of crop training data from China’s Sanjiang Plain region.

Unlike optical imagery, L-band radar emphasizes standing water and vegetation structure, so it can separate flooded rice from other crops. We used NISAR L2 GCOV HH and HV backscatter across the Sanjiang Plain, read as a season-long time series for every 20m pixel, to teach our model the rhythm of a crop season, applying masked pretraining to minimize the need for labels. We compared it against traditional methods such as convolutional networks and gradient boosting using identical labeled pixels, scoring each on blocks of land it never trained on with the macro F1 metric.

At both 100 and 1,000 labeled pixels per crop, the pretrained model scored above the best standard method. With plentiful labels, the per-pixel models converged; our spatial transformer, trained on more labels, scored highest. When some of the season’s radar images were removed at random, as if the satellite had missed them, our model held up far better than gradient boosting trained only on complete seasons. We used the unchanged Sanjiang model in California with no local labels, and it found 90% of the rice on the most recent USDA crop map when the California images came from the same months the model had learned from, and its agreement score fell by 12 to 15 points when scans from outside that season were added.

The MaskSAR Explorer (https://masksar.web.app/) enables analysts, researchers, educators, and learners to inspect sample locations’ radar history beside the reference label, a model prediction score, and dated Sentinel-2 images. Every layer follows one chain: the NISAR observation, the processing applied to it, the historical reference or model output, what the user can inspect, and the strongest conclusion that evidence supports. Exploratory layers from a separate pipeline are labelled as such, and the app never presents model agreement as verified 2026 ground truth.

Our project matters because it demonstrates the advantages of pretrained crop models in areas without recent and accurate data labels, and recognises when traditional methods are sufficient. Masked pretraining of satellite time series is established for optical imagery (SITS-BERT, U-BARN, Presto) and has recently reached C-band Sentinel-1 (SAR2Agri, SAR-TS-BERT). We did not invent the method; we asked a question those papers do not answer on a sensor they do not use: on NISAR’s L-band time series, under how few labels, with how many scans missing, and across which calendars does it still help?

We have personal connections to the region as two of our team members’ parents are from Northeast China, home of the Sanjiang Plain. This is family heritage only: MaskSAR is independent student work with no affiliation to any organization in China. Our testing region, the Sacramento Valley, is close to home: our school is in the Sacramento area, and the valley’s rice fields are part of the landscape we grew up near.

Scores compare models with historical crop maps, not verified 2026 field conditions. AI assistants helped write code and text; the team chose the question, methods and every claim, and all numbers come from logged result files. Every number traces to checksummed result files and pinned code revisions, and 675 pixel-identity checks confirmed that matched baselines used exactly the neural models’ fitting pixels.

Research Paper: https://masksar.web.app/data/masksar.pdf. 

The research pipeline is written in Python: h5py and rasterio read NISAR GCOV granules from the Alaska Satellite Facility, GDAL and NumPy handle gridding and quality masking, and PyTorch and LightGBM train the models on NVIDIA L40S GPUs on MIT’s ORCD Engaging cluster. The app is written in JavaScript, using MapLibre GL for the interactive maps, PMTiles to stream radar layers in the browser, and three.js with 3d-tiles-renderer for 3D terrain, and is hosted on Firebase, so it needs no login or installation. Every inspector score is an out-of-fold prediction from the controlled study, missing scan dates are shown as gaps rather than filled in, and all data are precomputed static files.
projectRefs: NISAR crop-area algorithm, Anconitano et al. (2024)
